passage: Counsellor's note. In the reading group, Ankita was asked to tell us about the story we had all read. She started, “First the boy found a lamp, and then there was a shop, and then his mother was worried, and then…” and stopped, tangled. I asked, “What is the one thing that matters most?” She thought and said, “The boy kept the lamp safe.” Then she added, “Sorry, the middle part wasn't clear.” I told her that it is a good habit to say so, and that I too sometimes lose my way. Next time we will list three key points first. Ms. Jyoti.

qa.q: What did Ankita say was not clear?
qa.a: The middle part.

qa.q: What was Ankita probably feeling when she stopped, tangled in her summary?
qa.a: She was likely a bit flustered, and her apology shows she was aware her middle part was muddled.

qa.q: What method does the counsellor plan to use next time?
qa.a: Ms. Jyoti plans to have the group list three key points first, to help choose what matters.

qa.q: How might the other children in the group benefit from hearing this exchange?
qa.a: They see that an adult also loses the way and admits it, so they may feel safer saying when something is unclear.

grounding: A child learns to summarise a story in a few lines and to clarify a muddled point, and adults model admitting when something was not clear.

passage: Friday night diary. Today Miss Parul asked us to tell the class about our library book in only three sentences. I usually talk on and on! I wrote mine: “Ravi finds a lost puppy. He asks everyone in the colony whose it is. In the end he keeps it because nobody comes.” Miss said it was clear. Then I explained the part about the ladder, and Parul said, “I still don't get that,” and I realised I hadn't told it well. I said, “Oh, I'll say it again,” and did. Mummy says it's okay not to be perfect. I'll try three sentences again tomorrow. Vasudha.

qa.q: How many sentences did Miss Parul ask for?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt when Parul did not get the part about the ladder?
qa.a: Vasudha was probably a little disappointed at not telling it well, but calm enough to say, "Oh, I'll say it again."

qa.q: What could Vasudha try to do next to improve future summaries?
qa.a: Vasudha could pick the key points first, keep to three sentences and be ready to clarify a muddled part.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt when asking about the ladder?
qa.a: Parul was probably curious and wanted to follow the story, and asking helped Vasudha see what was unclear.

grounding: A child learns to summarise a story in three sentences and to clarify a muddled point.

passage: In the hill village school, Hafsa Teacher asked Tenzin to tell the class the story his grandfather had told him about the lost yak. Tenzin started, and went on, and on: the snow, the prayer flags, his grandfather's boots, the other yaks, what they had for dinner. After five minutes the class was fidgeting. Hafsa Teacher raised a hand. “It's a lovely story. Can you give it to us in three lines? Who, what went wrong, how it ended.” Tenzin frowned, counting on his fingers. “A yak got lost in the snow. Grandfather followed its bell for a whole night. He found it sheltering by the monastery wall.” The class clapped.

qa.q: Where did Grandfather find the yak?
qa.a: He found it sheltering by the monastery wall.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling as he counted on his fingers?
qa.a: Tenzin was concentrating hard and maybe a little unsure, working out which parts of the long story mattered most.

qa.q: How did Hafsa Teacher help Tenzin summarise?
qa.a: She praised the story and gave a simple frame, who, what went wrong and how it ended, to pick out the key points.

qa.q: What was the long version like for the class?
qa.a: The class grew restless and fidgety, losing the thread in all the extra details.

grounding: Shows a child learning to summarise a long story in three lines, with an adult modelling how to choose key points.

passage: Mr Anders Lund had spent ten minutes explaining the water cycle to his class in Oslo, drawing arrows all over the board until it looked like spaghetti. He stopped and laughed. “I've made that very confusing, haven't I? Sorry. Who can help me say it in three steps?” Clara looked at the mess of arrows and felt her brain untangle it. She put up her hand. “Water goes up as vapour. It makes clouds. It comes down as rain.” Mr Lund wiped the board clean and wrote her three lines. “That's clearer than I was. Thank you, Clara.” Clara felt her cheeks go warm.

qa.q: How long had Mr Lund spent explaining?
qa.a: He had spent ten minutes explaining the water cycle.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling when Mr Lund thanked her?
qa.a: Clara felt pleased and a little shy, her cheeks going warm at the praise.

qa.q: What did Mr Lund model for the class?
qa.a: He modelled admitting that his explanation was confusing and then choosing a few key points to make it clear.

qa.q: How might the class have felt before Clara's summary?
qa.a: The class was probably confused by the spaghetti of arrows and relieved when it became three simple steps.

grounding: Shows an adult admitting a muddled explanation and a child summarising it in a few key points.

passage: At the hostel's Sunday meeting, the warden explained new rules about phone time, laundry days and the study room. Amandeep had been at the doctor and missed it. At dinner he asked Vishal, “What did I miss?” Vishal waved his fork. “Loads. Phones something, laundry changed, and the study room, um, closes, or opens…” Amandeep looked more confused. Vishal stopped. “Wait. Let me do it properly.” He counted on his fingers. “One: phones only after dinner. Two: laundry is Wednesday now, not Monday. Three: the study room stays open till ten.” Then he added, “The laundry bit I'm not sure about. Let's check the notice board.” It said Wednesday.

qa.q: What day is laundry now?
qa.a: Laundry is on Wednesday now, not Monday.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he stopped and said “Wait”?
qa.a: Vishal felt a little embarrassed at the muddled first answer and determined to get it right for Amandeep.

qa.q: What did Vishal do well the second time?
qa.a: He picked out three key points, counted them clearly, and admitted which one he wasn't sure about so they could check.

qa.q: Why was Amandeep relying on Vishal?
qa.a: Amandeep had missed the meeting because he was at the doctor, so he needed a clear summary.

grounding: Shows a child clarifying a muddled summary by choosing key points and admitting what was not clear.

passage:
I'm Saurabh, and I sit next to Tanvir in English. Yesterday Miss Fernandes asked him to tell the class what happened in the story we'd read, in three sentences. Tanvir took a breath and went on for about five minutes: the dog, the bus, the aunt's umbrella, the other dog, the part where the bus came back. People started yawning.

Miss Fernandes stopped him kindly. "Lots of detail, Tanvir. And honestly, I explained the ending badly yesterday, so that's partly my fault. Let's pick the key points together: who, what went wrong, how it ended."

Tanvir scrunched his face. "The boy lost his dog on the bus, everyone searched, and the dog came back on the next bus." Miss clapped. I don't know if he was embarrassed, but he sat down smiling.

qa.q: How many sentences was Tanvir asked to use?
qa.a: Three sentences.

qa.q: What might Tanvir have been feeling when he sat down smiling?
qa.a: Probably proud and relieved that his short summary worked, though Saurabh can't be sure whether he was also embarrassed.

qa.q: What did Miss Fernandes model that helped Tanvir?
qa.a: She admitted her own unclear explanation and showed how to pick key points: who, what went wrong and how it ended.

qa.q: How did the listening class experience Tanvir's first summary?
qa.a: The long list of details lost them, and people started yawning.

grounding: It is a classmate's account of a child learning to summarise a story in a few lines, with a teacher modelling key points and admitting her own unclear part.
